title: Climate Tipping Points
scope: Thresholds in the Earth system that trigger self-perpetuating change.

overview.summary: Whether Earth holds thresholds that flip irreversibly once crossed, and whether naming them sharpens or muddies climate action.
overview.scope_covered: Earth-system thresholds: abruptness, irreversibility, early-warning signals, cascade risk, and what tipping language does to policy and publics.
overview.scope_excluded: general warming attribution, mitigation policy design, geoengineering, and social or political tipping dynamics in their own right.
overview.why_now: A 2025 global scientific assessment declared warm-water coral reefs the first tipping element already crossing its threshold, sharpening dispute over how solid, and how useful, such declarations are.

stats.label: Global warming so far · vs Paris Agreement limits
stats.note: 2024 ran about 1.55°C above the 1850-1900 average — the warmest year on record, boosted by El Niño. The Paris 1.5°C goal is a multi-decade average and has not been passed; 2°C is the outer limit.
stats.detail: The World Meteorological Organization dates this to a single calendar year, boosted by a strong El Niño; one warm year does not itself mean the Paris Agreement’s longer-run 1.5°C goal, measured as a multi-decade average, has been missed. IPCC AR6 put the more conservative 2011-2020 decadal average at 1.09°C above pre-industrial. Either way, several tipping-element threshold ranges begin at or just above the warming level already reached.

stats.label: Tipping elements with a threshold within 1.5°C
stats.note: Four of 16 elements — both polar ice sheets, warm-water coral reefs and abrupt permafrost thaw — have thresholds at or below 1.5°C on best estimates, which carry wide ranges; a crossed threshold plays out over decades to millennia.
stats.detail: The uncertainty is substantial: Greenland’s ice-sheet threshold is best-estimated at 1.5°C but plausibly sits anywhere from 0.8°C to 3°C. The assessment is Armstrong-McKay et al. (2022, Science), which assigns each element a best-estimate threshold with an explicit uncertainty range rather than a single trigger temperature.

stats.label: Coral reefs exposed to bleaching-level heat · fourth global event (2023-2025)
stats.note: 84% of the world’s coral reef area met bleaching-level heat stress during the fourth global mass-bleaching event on record, which ran from early 2023 to mid-2025.
stats.detail: The event reached reefs in all three coral-bearing ocean basins, the Pacific, the Atlantic and the Indian, across at least 83 countries and territories, with mortality reaching up to 93% at some sites, such as reefs off Mexico’s Pacific coast, according to the International Coral Reef Initiative. NOAA Coral Reef Watch announced in June 2026 that the event had likely ended in mid-2025, after no widespread bleaching was reported through the following austral summer. Coral bleaching is one of the few tipping-relevant shifts already visibly underway rather than only projected, though bleached coral can sometimes recover if heat stress eases quickly enough.
stats.source_label: NOAA NESDIS / Coral Reef Watch; International Coral Reef Initiative

stats.label: Amazon deforestation · vs estimated dieback threshold
stats.note: About 20% of the Amazon has been cleared and another 6% heavily degraded, 26% in all. The estimated threshold sits at 20-25% deforestation, past which much of the eastern and southern basin flips to degraded savanna.
stats.detail: The threshold estimate comes from ecologists Carlos Nobre and Thomas Lovejoy (Science Advances, 2018), who combined deforestation with climate-driven drying and fire risk; deforestation alone, absent added climate stress, would need to reach roughly 40% to trigger the same shift. The cleared and degraded shares come from Amazonia Against the Clock, the 2022 regional assessment organised by COICA with Stand.earth and research by RAISG. Brazil’s annual deforestation rate has fallen sharply since 2023 under renewed enforcement, which slows the approach to the threshold but does not reduce the area already cleared.
stats.source_label: Amazonia Against the Clock (COICA / Stand.earth, research by RAISG, 2022) for cleared and degraded area; Lovejoy & Nobre, Science Advances for the threshold

stats.label: Identified tipping elements · Earth system
stats.note: Sixteen large-scale parts of the Earth system are judged capable of shifting into a new, self-sustaining state once a threshold is crossed.
stats.detail: The count comes from Armstrong-McKay et al. (2022, Science), which synthesized decades of tipping-element research into a peer-reviewed assessment with best-estimate and uncertainty-range warming thresholds for each. Nine are core elements whose tipping would have consequences reaching well beyond their own region, such as ice sheets and ocean circulation; seven are regional-impact elements, such as coral reefs and boreal forest, whose effects concentrate more locally even though the underlying warming driving them is global.

stats.label: Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) · observed slowdown
stats.note: The current has weakened by roughly 15-20% since the mid-20th century, a loss of about 0.46 Sverdrups (millions of cubic metres of water per second) per decade. IPCC AR6 dropped from high to medium its confidence that a collapse before 2100 can be ruled out.
stats.detail: How close the AMOC sits to an actual tipping threshold is genuinely contested among specialists: a 2023 study (Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen) used sea-surface-temperature proxies to project a central collapse estimate around mid-century, with a wide 95% uncertainty range, while other researchers judged the underlying proxy record too short to support that specific date. A February 2025 high-resolution modeling study concluded a full collapse this century remains unlikely. IPCC AR6 (2021) itself states only that a 21st-century collapse is not its central expectation, held at medium confidence.
stats.source_label: Pontes & Menviel, Nature Geoscience trend estimate; IPCC AR6 WG1 for collapse confidence

stats.label: Sea-level rise potential · if each ice sheet were fully lost
stats.note: Losing any one ice sheet in full would eventually add meters to global sea level, though the trigger and the centuries-to-millennia unfolding are separate questions.
stats.detail: These are eventual sea-level contributions if an ice sheet were lost in full, not a near-term forecast: even once a threshold is passed, Greenland’s loss is projected to play out over roughly 1,000 to 15,000 years and West Antarctica’s over roughly 500 to 13,000 years, depending on the pathway. East Antarctica is considered far more stable and is not among the ice sheets assessed as having a near-term threshold.
stats.source_label: IPCC AR6 WG1; Armstrong-McKay et al., Science

stats.label: Tipping cascades in model simulations · at 2°C warming
stats.note: Across about 3.7 million simulations of four interacting tipping elements, two or more tipped together in roughly 27% of runs even with warming capped at 2°C.
stats.detail:
The 2021 study modeled documented interaction pathways between four elements, the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Atlantic overturning circulation and the Amazon rainforest, rather than observing cascades directly, so the result describes model behavior under assumed linkages, not a measured real-world frequency. In the model the ice sheets are usually the initiators and the overturning circulation the mediator: Greenland or West Antarctic melt weakens the circulation, which then carries the disturbance on to the Amazon.

The 27% is derived at the strongest assumed coupling, where 61% of runs tip at all and 44% of those tipping runs involve two or more elements; cascades become rarer as the assumed coupling between elements is weakened, and at the weakest coupling tested no multi-element cascades occur at all. Researchers differ on how much weight such a finding should carry for policy, which is precisely the live question of how to treat a low-probability, high-consequence, hard-to-verify risk.
stats.source_label: Wunderling et al., Earth System Dynamics

questions.text: How close is the Atlantic overturning circulation to a threshold, and can current models resolve that distance?
questions.why: Proxy and observational signals hint the Atlantic current system that carries warm water north sits closer to a critical slowdown than official assessments allow, but those assessments rest on models that critics say are biased toward stability.
questions.detail: The direct instrumental record (the RAPID monitoring array) is only about two decades long, too short to confirm a long-term trend with confidence. Paleoclimate and sea-surface-temperature proxies point to a subpolar Atlantic weakening and cooling pattern since the mid-20th century, and some researchers report statistical early-warning fingerprints (rising variance, slower recovery from perturbations) consistent with an approaching critical transition. Against this, the multi-model ensembles underlying mainstream assessments show continued gradual weakening through the century but assign low likelihood to outright collapse, a conclusion critics say is undermined by well-documented freshwater-forcing biases that make these models artificially stable. The dispute is less about direction (virtually everyone agrees the AMOC is weakening) and more about whether the models used to reassure policymakers are trustworthy enough to rule out a much closer, sharper threshold.

questions.text: Are major ice-sheet losses already committed at today’s warming, or still avoidable by rapid mitigation?
questions.why: Ice loss is accelerating past what earlier projections assumed, and self-sustaining retreat may already be under way at glaciers like Thwaites, but how much of the eventual rise is locked in rather than still emissions-sensitive is unresolved.
questions.detail:
Gravimetry and altimetry data show mass loss from both ice sheets accelerating over the past two decades, exceeding prior projection ranges, and marine ice-sheet and ice-cliff instability mechanisms give a physical basis for retreat that continues even without further warming once triggered; some paleoclimate reconstructions show past interglacial ice sheets shedding metres of sea-level-equivalent ice over centuries once destabilized. Those emphasizing commitment point to studies suggesting key West Antarctic outlet glaciers may already be in irreversible retreat.

Those emphasizing continued avoidability note that process-based ice-sheet models remain highly uncertain about the timing and magnitude of the ice-cliff and hydrofracturing mechanisms specifically, that most peer-reviewed projections still show a wide range of 21st-century outcomes strongly dependent on emissions pathway, and that rapid decarbonization measurably slows the rate and reduces the eventual extent of loss even where some commitment already exists. Nearly everyone agrees some future sea-level rise is already baked in; the argument is over how large that committed fraction is relative to what mitigation can still change.

questions.text: Should policy weight low-probability, irreversible catastrophes far above their expected-value harm?
questions.why: Mainstream climate economics weights a catastrophe by its small probability, while precautionary reasoning says a potentially unbounded, irreversible loss breaks that math and justifies heavy insurance now.
questions.detail: Integrated assessment models built on expected-value logic have historically given catastrophic tipping-point damages little weight because they contribute a small share of the probability-weighted mean outcome; critics working in a fat-tail or dismal-theorem tradition argue that when a loss distribution is unbounded and irreversible, expected-value math is the wrong tool, and society should behave more like it is buying insurance against ruin than optimizing an average. Opponents of the heavy-tail-weighting view counter that this reasoning, taken to its logical end, can justify near-unlimited present sacrifice for arbitrarily small probabilities, is not decision-theoretically tractable, and risks crowding out other urgent priorities; they also note that newer integrated assessment models increasingly build tipping-point damages into their central estimates rather than abandoning expected-value framing outright. This is a genuine fork in risk philosophy and intergenerational ethics, not simply a modeling dispute that better data would resolve.

questions.text: Does tipping-point framing mobilize the public and policymakers, or breed fatalism and confusion?
questions.why: Threshold warnings raise perceived urgency in some studies and, in others, leave audiences feeling the outcome is already locked in, or the science visibly unsettled.
questions.detail: Experimental studies on concrete, threshold-framed messaging (“tipping point,” “point of no return”) sometimes show it raises perceived issue urgency and short-term willingness to back policy, consistent with the general finding that vivid, bounded risks mobilize people more than diffuse, gradual ones. Other studies and communicator surveys report a backfire risk: audiences told catastrophe is already being locked in report reduced agency and increased fatalism, and can grow distrustful when the precise threshold or date does not play out as stated, especially since scientists themselves visibly disagree on the exact figures, which can read to skeptical audiences as the science being unsettled or overstated. Communication researchers broadly agree the effect hinges on pairing: threshold framing combined with a clear, feasible response tends to mobilize, while threshold framing alone, or paired with “it’s already too late” messaging, tends toward fatalism. No clean consensus exists on which effect dominates in aggregate public response.

questions.text: Can early-warning signals reliably detect an approaching threshold soon enough to act on it?
questions.why: Theory predicts statistical warning signs before a system tips, and researchers report some in ocean and paleoclimate data, but real records are too short and noisy to turn a signal into a usable lead time.
questions.detail: Critical-slowing-down theory, developed in dynamical systems and validated in ecological and some paleoclimate settings, predicts measurable precursors before a system approaches a bifurcation, and some studies report such signals in proxy records preceding past abrupt shifts and in recent ocean-circulation datasets, offering a scientific basis for real-time monitoring. Skeptics note the method was largely developed and tested on well-sampled or idealized systems, whereas real Earth subsystems have short, sparse, and noisy observational records that make any detected signal hard to distinguish from natural variability; even where a signal is credible, converting it into a specific lead time or crossing probability is not yet possible with confidence; and some transitions may be triggered abruptly by external shocks rather than unfolding as a slow approach to a bifurcation, which the framework does not cover. The honest assessment is that early-warning detection is a promising diagnostic tool under active development, not yet an operational alarm system policymakers can rely on.

questions.text: Would crossing one threshold materially raise the odds of cascading others?
questions.why: Physical links between elements are plausible, and network models find one crossing lowers the bar for the next, but the coupling strengths driving that result come from simplified models rather than validated Earth-system simulations.
questions.detail: Candidate physical pathways between tipping elements are documented: AMOC weakening is projected to shift precipitation patterns that stress the Amazon, and Greenland meltwater could itself weaken the AMOC, creating plausible feedback loops. Network-theoretic studies that represent the climate system as a set of coupled tipping elements find that interactions can lower the effective tipping threshold of connected elements, sometimes substantially, lending scientific weight to a cascade or domino narrative that now appears alongside the more established single-element literature. Skeptics counter that the quantitative coupling strengths driving these results come from simplified conceptual models rather than fully validated Earth-system simulations, that the sign of some interactions may be stabilizing rather than destabilizing, and that headline cascade-risk figures often trace back to a small number of studies rather than a broad, converged literature. Researchers broadly treat cascade risk as scientifically credible in principle while acknowledging it remains among the least quantitatively constrained parts of tipping-point science.

questions.text: Is harm that is irreversible on multi-century timescales morally different from severe but recoverable damage?
questions.why: One tradition holds that permanently foreclosing future generations’ options is worse in kind, another that only the scale of suffering counts, not whether the damage is classed as reversible.
questions.detail: Precautionary and some deontological traditions in environmental ethics argue irreversibility carries independent moral weight because it removes the possibility of correction or restitution and permanently forecloses choices for every generation that follows, making it worse in kind, not just degree, than recoverable harm however severe. A welfarist or straightforwardly consequentialist view counters that what matters morally is the total magnitude and distribution of harm and suffering, and that from the standpoint of anyone living through the consequences, a severe harm recoverable only after many centuries is practically indistinguishable from one labeled permanently irreversible. A middle position treats irreversibility as mattering instrumentally, because it removes future option value and compounds uncertainty, rather than as a separate moral category in its own right. The disagreement is a genuine values fork in intergenerational ethics, not something further evidence resolves.

positions.name: Tipping Point Sentinel
positions.steelman: Some of these doors are already closing, and once shut they do not reopen.
positions.description: When a change is irreversible on human timescales, waiting for statistical certainty means finding out only after the door has shut. The 2022 Science assessment led by David Armstrong McKay found five of sixteen tipping elements, including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, warm-water coral reefs and Labrador Sea convection, with estimated thresholds already within reach at today’s roughly 1.2 to 1.4°C of warming. Coral makes the case hardest to wave away: the 2025 Global Tipping Points report, coordinated by 160 authors under Tim Lenton at the University of Exeter, documents reefs already in unprecedented dieback at 1.4°C, decades ahead of what policy planning assumed. These are not costs that scale smoothly with degrees warmed, they are switches with hysteresis built in, and a switch, once thrown, does not un-throw itself just because emissions later fall.
positions.detail:
The concept has a real scientific lineage, not a recent activist coinage. Tim Lenton, Stefan Rahmstorf, Hans Joachim Schellnhuber and colleagues formalized “tipping elements” in a landmark 2008 PNAS paper identifying nine large-scale Earth systems capable of qualitative, self-sustaining shifts once forced past a threshold. The field has matured since: the 2022 Science paper by Armstrong McKay, Lenton, Rockström and others assigned each element a best-estimate and range of warming thresholds, and the 2025 Global Tipping Points report scaled that into the largest expert assessment yet, endorsed through the Dartington Declaration by over 640 scientists. Sentinels read that trajectory as consensus hardening toward their position, not away from it: the more carefully these systems get modeled, the more of them turn out to have plausible thresholds at or near where the world already stands.

The internal debate among Sentinels is less about whether abrupt, irreversible thresholds exist and more about how close the worst ones are. The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) is the sharpest fight: the direct observational record from the RAPID array only starts in 2004, so the central estimate for collapse sits well above today’s warming even as some paleoclimate reconstructions and simplified models push it much lower. In October 2024, 44 climate scientists, including Stefan Rahmstorf, signed an open letter to the Nordic Council of Ministers warning that AMOC collapse risk this century has been systematically underestimated and could arrive within decades, not centuries. Sentinels treat that disagreement as itself the argument for urgency: a risk this consequential does not need a tight consensus estimate to justify acting on the low end of the range, and ice sheet science has already shown a pattern of underestimating pace, from Antarctic outlet glaciers now assessed as possibly past self-sustaining retreat.

The proponents driving this framing into policy are not fringe: Tim Lenton’s Global Systems Institute, Johan Rockström’s planetary boundaries work at the Potsdam Institute, Stefan Rahmstorf on ocean circulation, and James Hansen’s long record of early warnings on ice sheet instability all converge on the same structural claim, that committed, hysteresis-locked change is qualitatively different from ordinary damage and has to be governed differently. Their sharpest internal worry is not that the science is wrong but that policy language has not caught up: cost-benefit frameworks built for smooth, marginal damages systematically underprice discontinuous, irreversible ones, and by the time observational proof of a crossed threshold arrives, in Sentinel terms, it is already too late for that proof to do any good.
positions.proponents: Tim Lenton, Johan Rockström, Stefan Rahmstorf, David Armstrong McKay, Hans Joachim Schellnhuber, James Hansen
positions.representative_name: Tim Lenton / Global Tipping Points report
positions.representative_note: Leads the Global Systems Institute at the University of Exeter and coordinated the 2023 and 2025 Global Tipping Points reports, the largest expert assessments of Earth-system thresholds to date.

positions.name: Continuum Realist
positions.steelman: Thresholds are real but slow and regional — the next tenth of a degree matters most.
positions.description: What counts is not whether a named threshold gets crossed but how much warming gets avoided, degree by degree, because damage keeps scaling long after any headline number passes. Greenland’s ice sheet may cross an instability threshold somewhere between 0.8°C and 3°C of warming, yet the melt plays out over millennia rather than one catastrophic decade, and the Met Office’s own modelling shows permafrost thaw behaving as a gradual, continuous feedback rather than a large-scale abrupt flip. Even the Atlantic overturning circulation, the poster child for abrupt collapse, is judged by IPCC assessments as unlikely to tip this century, and separate 2022 studies found the statistical methods behind collapse-by-mid-century headlines overstate the risk when tested against models whose behaviour is already known. None of that licenses complacency: it is the reason to treat every tenth of a degree of avoided warming as consequential in its own right.
positions.detail:
The tipping-elements idea traces to Lenton, Rahmstorf, Schellnhuber and colleagues’ 2008 PNAS survey of the Earth system’s potential switches, escalated by the 2019 Nature comment “Climate tipping points — too risky to bet against,” in which Lenton, Rockström, Rahmstorf and colleagues argued that nine of the fifteen tipping elements identified over the preceding decade might already be active. Continuum realists do not dispute the underlying physics so much as the rhetorical compression: naming a fixed list of “tipping elements” as if they were switches on one planetary control panel obscures that each operates on wildly different timescales and geographies, most of them centuries long and regionally bounded. The 2019 UN Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere is blunt about West Antarctica specifically: “observational data are not yet sufficient to determine whether these changes mark the beginning of irreversible retreat” — a live scientific question, not a foregone catastrophe.

The sharpest internal argument is the Atlantic overturning circulation. Peter and Susanne Ditlevsen’s 2023 statistical early-warning analysis put a central collapse estimate around mid-century within a 2025–2095 range, and a 2024 open letter signed by 44 scientists warned the risk had been “greatly underestimated.” Continuum realists, including Met Office scientists such as Richard Wood, counter that IPCC assessments still hold a 21st-century collapse “unlikely,” and that separate 2022 studies found the statistical fingerprinting methods behind Ditlevsen-style forecasts overstate collapse risk when applied to full climate models whose actual behaviour is already known. Nobody in this argument denies the AMOC is weakening; the dispute is whether “collapse” on a single date is the right unit of analysis, versus a continuous multi-decadal decline that is already doing worsening, measurable damage to European climate and West African monsoon rainfall well before any hypothetical shutdown.

Mat Collins, an IPCC lead author at Exeter, has noted the field remains unsettled on what should even count as a tipping point: a strict mathematical bifurcation, a policy-relevant threshold, or simply any bad outcome. Continuum realists take that unsettledness as reason to keep the policy conversation anchored to the one number that is scientifically uncontroversial and directly actionable, cumulative emissions and the warming trajectory they produce, rather than a debate over where exactly a handful of contested cliff-edges sit. That is also why this camp converges with the IPCC’s own operating framing, that every increment of warming avoided reduces risk, treating the location of specific thresholds as scientifically live but secondary to the case for faster mitigation now.
positions.proponents: Richard Wood, Mat Collins, Andy Wiltshire, Katharine Hayhoe, IPCC (AR6 Working Group I)
positions.representative_note: Leads Atlantic overturning circulation risk assessment for the UK Met Office; frames AMOC collapse as a genuine but low-probability, not-this-century risk rather than an imminent cliff-edge, consistent with IPCC AR6’s own confidence levels.

positions.name: Framing Critic
positions.steelman: One dramatic word stretched over unlike physics confuses more than it moves.
positions.description: Climate action needs language people can act on, and “tipping point” does not deliver it: gradual ice-sheet loss over centuries, a possible abrupt Atlantic circulation shift and regional ecosystem collapse all get welded under one dramatic label, erasing the distinctions policymakers actually need. A 2024 Nature Climate Change analysis by ten scientists, including IPCC lead author Michael Oppenheimer, concludes the framing “oversimplifies the diverse dynamics of complex natural and human systems” and can convey urgency “without fostering a meaningful basis for climate action.” Manjana Milkoreit’s 2023 review in WIREs Climate Change documents an “explosion of interest” in tipping-point language spreading well past where the science supports it, flagging four recurring patterns of overuse. The point is not that abrupt change is impossible: it is that treating every risk as a cliff-edge blurs what is truly irreversible and what is merely worsening, and that blur serves neither policy nor public understanding.
positions.detail:
The critique comes from inside climate science, not from skeptics of warming itself, which is what gives it teeth. Kopp, Gilmore, Shwom, Adams, Adler, Oppenheimer, Patwardhan, Russill, Schmidt and York argue in their Nature Climate Change paper (published online December 2024) that the tipping-point umbrella term collapses genuinely distinct dynamics, abrupt physical thresholds, slow-moving commitments already locked in, social and economic regime shifts, into a single metaphor borrowed from everyday experience (a glass tipping over) that implies a speed and finality the underlying science frequently can’t support. They warn this can backfire two ways: it can suggest that anything short of preventing every threshold is failure, breeding fatalism once a “point” is thought crossed, or it can invite complacency because the threshold always seems to recede into an uncertain future rather than demanding a specific near-term action.

Milkoreit’s WIREs Climate Change review, examining how “social tipping points” in particular have proliferated as a proposed lever for rapid decarbonization, catalogs deleterious patterns including premature labeling of ordinary social change as a tipping dynamic, and cautions that stretching a precise dynamical-systems concept to cover diffuse social processes drains it of analytical and communicative value. Mike Hulme, the Cambridge geographer known for scrutinizing the rhetoric of climate discourse, has separately argued that treating climate change as fundamentally a problem of incremental, cumulative harm gets closer to the policy-relevant truth than a “false emphasis on immediacy and abruptness.” None of this denies that abrupt regional shifts (an ice shelf collapse, a coral die-off) occur; the argument is that naming everything a tipping point doesn’t sharpen the science communicated to the public or the levers available to policymakers, it flattens them, and that flattening carries its own cost when it either paralyzes or is later seen to have cried wolf.
positions.proponents: Robert E. Kopp, Michael Oppenheimer, Manjana Milkoreit, Mike Hulme
positions.representative_name: Kopp et al., “‘Tipping points’ confuse and can distract from urgent climate action,” Nature Climate Change (2024/2025)
positions.representative_note: Ten-author critique co-signed by IPCC lead author Michael Oppenheimer, arguing the tipping-point umbrella oversimplifies distinct physical and social dynamics and can convey urgency without giving people an actionable basis for climate response

positions.name: Fat-Tail Insurer
positions.steelman: You don’t need to know the odds of the house burning down to buy fire insurance.
positions.description: Climate policy is a risk-management problem before it is a cost-benefit problem: when the distribution of outcomes has a fat tail, expected-value economics quietly averages a low but real chance of civilization-scale damage into a small, comfortable number. Martin Weitzman’s ‘dismal theorem’ showed that under deep uncertainty about climate sensitivity, the tail of possible outcomes does not thin out fast enough for expected costs to converge at all, so it can dominate the entire calculation. That is not hypothetical: IPCC’s own AR6 assessment still cannot rule out equilibrium climate sensitivity well above its 2.5 to 4°C best-estimate range, and the prior generation of models ran as high as 5.6°C. Price the premium to the worst plausible loss rather than the likeliest one, which is exactly what reinsurers already do, with Munich Re data showing weather-catastrophe payouts running roughly five times higher than the 1980s average.
positions.detail:
This case was formalized by Martin Weitzman in 2009 and popularized with Gernot Wagner in the 2015 book Climate Shock: an ordinary household buys fire insurance without ever computing the precise odds its house burns down this year; it insures because the downside is large and irreversible, not because it has priced the risk to three decimal places. Climate sensitivity, the amount of warming per doubling of CO2, is exactly this kind of quantity: nobody can pin it to a single number, and the uncertainty is asymmetric, skewed toward nastier surprises rather than pleasant ones. That asymmetry is the whole argument. It is not a claim that catastrophe is likely; it is a claim that the possibility cannot be shrunk to zero, and a rational actor prices insurance against exactly that kind of possibility.

The sharpest pushback has come from within economics itself. Weitzman and William Nordhaus argued for years over discount rates and over whether the dismal theorem, taken literally, implies society should be willing to pay almost anything to avoid a non-zero chance of ruin, a conclusion even Weitzman treated as a reductio rather than a policy prescription. The honest answer proponents give is that the theorem is a warning about model structure, not a formula: it says do not let a tidy expected-value spreadsheet quietly zero out the tail, size the insurance premium to the plausible worst case, then argue about the size, not about whether tail risk belongs in the calculation at all.

The strongest evidence that this is more than an academic quarrel is that the people whose job is pricing catastrophic risk for a living have already adopted the framing. Mark Carney, then governor of the Bank of England, told insurers at Lloyd’s of London in 2015 that climate change is a tragedy of the horizon precisely because its worst impacts sit beyond the planning cycles of markets, companies, and regulators, and laid out physical, liability, and transition risk as the three channels through which the tail could hit the financial system. Reinsurers have been repricing accordingly: Munich Re’s loss data, cited in that same speech, shows inflation-adjusted weather-catastrophe payouts running around five times higher over the past decade than the 1980s average. None of that requires resolving exactly where the AMOC threshold sits or how fast an ice sheet collapses; it only requires taking seriously that nobody can rule the worst cases out, which is the one thing insurers are paid never to do.
positions.proponents: Martin Weitzman, Gernot Wagner, Mark Carney, Robert Pindyck
positions.representative_note: NYU climate economist; co-authored Climate Shock (Princeton University Press, 2015) with Weitzman, the fullest public statement of the fat-tail insurance case for climate action.

positions.name: Threshold Skeptic
positions.steelman: The physics keeps pointing to slow and survivable, not sudden and catastrophic.
positions.description: Good climate policy rests on what the evidence supports, not on whichever mechanism produces the most dramatic model run. Marine ice-cliff instability, the process behind the most extreme Antarctic sea-level scenarios, has never been observed in nature and appears in only a handful of simulations; when Edwards and colleagues (Nature, 2019) re-ran the paleoclimate record without assuming it, past sea-level rise no longer required it. The IPCC’s AR6 assessment rates an abrupt Atlantic overturning collapse before 2100 as unlikely at medium confidence, and even where a genuine threshold exists, as in the Greenland ice sheet, its own dynamics unfold over centuries to millennia rather than years. Overselling abruptness does not speed the response; it spends credibility that is better saved for the slow, unglamorous work of cutting emissions and building adaptive capacity now.
positions.detail:
The tipping-point vocabulary itself is young: Lenton and colleagues catalogued nine climate tipping elements in 2008, and by the time Lenton, Rockström and coauthors declared a planetary emergency in a 2019 Nature comment, the term had migrated from a technical description of bistable systems into a general-purpose word for anything alarming. Critics of that migration are not disputing that warming is real or damaging; they are disputing that the paleoclimate record actually shows a system perched on knife-edges. Read across ice ages, hyperthermals and interglacials, the Earth system has absorbed forcing changes many times larger than anything projected for this century without runaway collapse, which is itself evidence for a system with more stabilizing feedbacks than emergency framing allows.

The clearest case is Antarctica. Marine ice-cliff instability, the mechanism behind the highest-end 2016 projections of meters of sea-level rise this century, requires ice shelves to fail within roughly an hour once unbuttressed, something that has never been observed and that later work showed is checked by ice-debris buildup at the cliff face. A 2023 reanalysis of Last Interglacial sea level put the rise at around 2.7 metres, achievable without invoking the instability at all. The Atlantic overturning circulation tells a similar story: two independent 2022 studies found that the models most prone to predicting collapse tend to be the ones carrying known circulation biases, and the widely reported 2023 Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen forecast of collapse as early as 2025 leaned on a single subpolar-gyre proxy record that most oceanographers do not consider representative of the whole overturning system.

None of this is a claim that nothing changes: Greenland ice loss is self-reinforcing once elevation feedback kicks in, permafrost carbon is a genuine long-run risk, and warming itself is not in question. The argument is narrower and, proponents say, more honest: a threshold that plays out over centuries, like Greenland’s, is a different policy object than a cliff edge that plays out over years, and collapsing that distinction under one dramatic word invites either paralysis or the credibility loss that follows when a headlined collapse date quietly does not arrive. Judith Curry has pressed this point longest and most directly, arguing that near-term-apocalypse framing narrows the policy conversation rather than sharpening it. Bjørn Lomborg has built a public case, in False Alarm and after, that panic is a worse guide to climate policy than calibrated, adaptive response. Notably, the modeling that pulled the worst Antarctic scenarios back toward the mainstream came from researchers who themselves argue for rapid mitigation, Tamsin Edwards and colleagues among them, which proponents read as the correction arriving from inside the mainstream rather than against it.
positions.representative_note: Former chair of the School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at Georgia Tech; argues that the evidence points to slow, manageable change and that near-term-catastrophe framing narrows the policy conversation rather than sharpening it.

crux.lead: If the thresholds can’t be placed, is that the strongest case to act — or the weakest?
crux.subtitle: The camps split less on whether thresholds exist than on what uncertainty licenses: an emergency footing, an insurance premium, per-tenth-of-a-degree accounting, a calmer forecast, or different words entirely.
crux.empirical: Whether observation can shrink the fog: can models resolve the AMOC’s distance to its threshold, do early-warning signals give usable lead time, and are ice-sheet losses committed at today’s warming or still avoidable? The framing dispute is testable too: whether tipping language mobilizes publics and policymakers or breeds fatalism has data of its own.
crux.values: Whether harm that is irreversible on multi-century timescales belongs in a different moral category from severe but recoverable damage — and if so, how much present cost a low-probability, unpriceable tail can command. Beneath the framing fight sits a second stake: whether public language should be tuned for accuracy or for motion, and who decides that trade.

actions.title: Global Tipping Points Report
actions.description: University of Exeter-led assessment by 160 scientists (2025) mapping which Earth-system tipping points sit closest to being crossed and what remains avoidable.

actions.title: Tipping Points Confuse Climate Action
actions.description: Peer-reviewed 2025 Nature Climate Change commentary arguing the tipping-point metaphor is now stretched over so many unlike phenomena that it obscures more than it clarifies for policy.

actions.title: Citizens’ Climate Lobby
actions.description: Grassroots network of 350-plus volunteer chapters lobbying for steady, bipartisan carbon-pricing policy built around incremental degrees of warming rather than catastrophe-framed campaigns.

actions.title: Fat-Tailed Climate Uncertainty
actions.description: Martin Weitzman’s foundational 2011 paper arguing that structural uncertainty about catastrophic climate outcomes should dominate cost-benefit policy calculus, the theoretical root of insurance-style precaution.

actions.title: AMOC Collapse Timing Uncertainty
actions.description: 2026 preprint showing that once modeling and data uncertainties are properly propagated, a widely cited AMOC-collapse prediction’s confidence interval stretches from decades to millennia.

actions.title: Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty
actions.description: International sign-on campaign, endorsed by the European Parliament, the WHO and over a million individuals, pushing governments toward a binding treaty phasing out coal, oil and gas.
